newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Sluggish P&U sales disappoint.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sluggish P&U sales disappoint.

text.p: Troubled U.S./Swedish drugs group Pharmacia & Upjohn served up a fresh disappointment to the market on Tuesday with a lower than expected second quarter profit, sluggish sales for new drugs and a bleak outlook for 1997.
Its shares recoiled from early gains to tumble 14.5 crowns on the report to 284 crowns in Stockholm, but steadied later once New York opened.
"It looks as if 1997 is a year lost," said analyst Ingemar Kihlstrom at Aros Securities.
P&U, created by the merger of Pharmacia of Sweden and U.S. Upjohn in 1995, posted a 33 percent fall in earnings per share (EPS) to $0.34 before nonrecurring items.
This was below market expectations of $0.36, which had themselves been slashed from as high as $0.50 in early July when the company issued the latest in a string of profit warnings.
P&U said it saw the negative sales and earnings trends continuing in the second half of the year.
Second quarter sales fell four percent to $1.70 billion, in stark contrast to the surging sales enjoyed by most P&U rivals.
Fred Hassan, the company's new chief executive who is seen as P&U's potential saviour, tried to inject some optimism into the market, repeating his expectations of a turnaround in 1998.
Analysts, however, were doubtful of any real recovery next year as the report showed slow sales for newer, high-margin products.
"The poor sales of new products is worrisome," one analyst said.
Sales of anti-glaucoma drug Xalatan rose to $38 million in the second quarter from $29 million in the first quarter, while colorectal cancer drug Camptosar fell to $38 million from $41.
"Camptosar and Xalatan were supposed to bridge the sales gap but one, Camptosar, has already peaked," said Kihlstrom.
"As sales of older products fall, you must compensate this gap with new drugs. Xalatan will have to do this along with Detrusitol which the company hopes will be approved this year."
If P&U is unable to get urine incontinence treatment Detrusitol approved by the year-end, the expected turnaround in 1998 could be delayed, Kihlstrom said.
Analysts were also disappointed to see that sales of P&U's largest drug, the growth hormone Genotropin, had not fared better.
Gentropin sales rose to $97 in the second quarter from $90 in the first quarter, but fell two percent in local currencies.
The company's large and protracted merger and restructuring charges have been dogging the profit and loss account, and analysts are counting on Hassan to come down hard on costs.
Hassan said restructuring would result in further job losses on top of the 4,100 positions cut since the 1995 merger.
"Obviously they need to do something about costs...but if you look at the long-term growth you cannot build that on cost savings but new drugs growth," one Stockholm-based analyst said.
P&U said it would make an announcement in the fourth quarter indicating how its latest restructuring and associated savings and costs were doing.

Compounding the gloom was a planned charge of 10-16 cents a share in the third quarter of 1997 for the merger of P&U's Pharmacia Biotech subsidiary with the life sciences division of British Amersham International Plc.
Some analysts saw this as another profit warning.
"Biotech only makes up about five percent of the total turnover and it's a very large charge on such a small turnover," Kihlstrom said.
"I see it as a warning to everybody to look over their estimates for the rest of the year."
